The result in question concerns the minimum number $N(S,x,r)$ of conjugates of an automorphism $x \in \operatorname{Aut}(S)$ of order $|x|>2$ needed to generate a subgroup whose order is divisible by a prime $r \mid |S|$ with $(r,|x|)=1$. 

When $|x|$ is odd (hence $x \in S$, since all outer automorphism groups of sporadic groups have order 1 or 2), the hardest prime to produce is $r=2$: one must generate an even-order subgroup—equivalently, produce an involution—from products of conjugates of an odd-order element. For most sporadic groups and most conjugacy classes, two or three suitably chosen conjugates of $x$ generate a subgroup containing an involution (often by generating a dihedral group or escaping into a subgroup with even order). 

However, there is precisely one triple $(S, x^S, r)$ across all sporadic groups where three conjugates always fail: the subgroup generated by any three conjugates of $x$ remains of odd order, so one requires a fourth conjugate to break out and obtain a subgroup of even order. This exceptional phenomenon occurs when the conjugacy class of the odd-order element $x$ is "trapped" in a configuration where triples cannot generate an involution, and the prime in question is the smallest (and hardest) coprime prime.

\boxed{2}
